newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. tells Iraq to come clean on past arms programs.
newsitem.headline: U.N. tells Iraq to come clean on past arms programs.

text.p: Rolf Ekeus, the chief U.N. arms inspector, on Friday called on Iraqi President Saddam Hussein's government to abandon "once and for all" ambitions to retain or acquire weapons of mass destruction.

In a major half-year report to the Security Council, Ekeus said remaining problems in ridding Iraq of dangerous arms were not technical but political. "Their solution requires a major political decision by Iraq's leadership to give up, once and for all, all capabilities and ambition to retain or acquire the proscribed weapons," the report concluded.

A clean bill of health by Ekeus, head of the U.N. special commission on ridding Iraq of weapons of mass destruction, is a key requirement before the embargo on Iraqi oil exports can be lifted entirely. Iraq has been under U.N. sanctions since its invasion of Kuwait in August 1990.
"The commission is continuing its work as it cannot state that Iraq has accounted for all weapons, components and capabilities," the report said.

Specifically, Ekeus said little remained unknown about Baghdad's nuclear, biological, chemical and ballistic missile potential, but what was unknown could still cause devastating damage and casualties.

If a single missile warhead were filled with anthrax, an infectious animal disease that can spread to humans, "millions of lethal doses could be spread in an attack on any city of the region," he said.
But he did not disclose any major arms programmes or materials discovered in the last six months.
The report also said Iraq was hindering the long-term monitoring system the commission set up to make sure Baghdad does not reacquire the dangerous arms.

"Iraq's deteriorating performance called into question its commitment to the monitoring process and that if the trend were not reversed it could result in a situation with political consequences, whereby monitoring could no longer be considered operational," Ekeus warned.
Much of the information on past programmes the inspectors have found or questioned came from governments who had delivered materials to Iraq for its past programmes.

But Ekeus said "a small number" of governments, which he did not name, had not responded to repeated and long-standing requests for information. He said it would be "most unfortunate" if this prevented the commission from being able to give Iraq clearance required for any lifting of sanctions.

Ekeus concluded that Iraq's performance in the past six months had been contradictory. On one hand, he said, Baghdad had provided almost no new disclosures on weapons. But at the same time Tareq Aziz, its deputy prime minister, had made major efforts to implement procedures agreed on by both sides, including inspections of some sensitive sites.
